"It's done through intermediaries," he said. "[Dulling] down the content, not having certain anchors, some of the hosts of our programs and talk shows." Musharraf's emergency order put several restrictions on the media, preventing journalists from expressing opinions prejudicial to "the ideology ... or integrity of Pakistan." Journalists are also restricted from covering suicide bombings and militant activity and could face three-year jail terms if they "ridicule" members of the government or armed forces. Almost a dozen journalists have been arrested. Musharraf has denied that his restrictions bar criticism, saying they only ask for responsibility in reporting. The editorial criticized Musharraf and the United States and Britain for continuing to support him. While many Pakistani journalists have protested the restrictions, some smaller television channels have complied with the government's restrictions. GEO and ARY have refused. "It seems most of the other channels have kowtowed in order to survive," Aslan said. Musharraf has said the emergency order improves stability and will foster peaceful parliamentary elections, which he has said he would like to see take place before January 9. **The Gulf Blackout: How Musharraf’s Emergency Rule Silenced Pakistan’s Free Press**

In November 2007, facing escalating political instability, a defiant judiciary, and mounting challenges to his military rule, Pakistani President General Pervez Musharraf declared a nationwide state of emergency. He suspended the constitution, purged the Supreme Court, and deployed security forces across major cities. However, the most immediate and aggressive front of this authoritarian crackdown was launched not on the streets, but against the airwaves. 

In a desperate bid to control the political narrative, the Musharraf regime orchestrated a sweeping blackout of independent news channels, targeting the nation’s premier private broadcasters, GEO-TV and ARY Digital. The resulting campaign of censorship would stretch far beyond Pakistan's national borders, exposing the fragile nature of press freedom in the Middle East and marking one of the darkest chapters in modern South Asian journalism.

### The Rise of Independent Media and the Emergency Crisis

To understand the severity of the 2007 crackdown, one must look at the media landscape of the early 2000s. Ironically, earlier in his tenure, Musharraf had liberalized Pakistan’s broadcast sector, giving rise to a booming private television industry. Networks like GEO-TV and ARY Digital quickly became Household names, broadcasting real-time news, aggressive talk shows, and investigative reports to millions. 

By 2007, these networks had become vital platforms for political debate. They extensively covered the "Lawyers’ Movement"—a massive civil resistance campaign calling for the restoration of deposed Chief Justice Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry—and provided unfiltered coverage of growing opposition to military rule. For a government striving to project absolute control, the unvarnished reporting of these networks was deemed an existential threat.

When Musharraf issued the Provisional Constitutional Order (PCO) on November 3, 2007, declaring emergency rule, local cable operators were immediately ordered to pull independent news channels off the air, replacing them with state-run propaganda and foreign entertainment broadcasts. 

### The Dubai Extraterritorial Crackdown

Deprived of domestic cable networks, Pakistani broadcasters relied on their international infrastructure. Both GEO-TV and ARY Digital operated out of Dubai Media City in the United Arab Emirates, using Dubai as a safe hub to uplink their satellite transmissions to millions of viewers in the Middle East, Europe, North America, and across South Asia. 

Realizing that domestic blockades were insufficient to suppress the news, the Musharraf regime exerted intense diplomatic pressure on the UAE government. In an unprecedented move, Dubai authorities capitulated to Islamabad’s demands. On November 17, 2007, UAE regulators ordered GEO-TV and ARY Digital to shut down their operations in Dubai Media City.

The enforcement was swift and ruthless. Foreign uplink facilities were turned off, effectively severing the networks' international broadcasting capabilities. Overnight, millions of overseas Pakistanis and international observers were plunged into a news blackout, unable to access independent reporting on the military government's actions. The shutdown sent shockwaves through the global media community, raising alarm over how easily authoritarian regimes could extend their censorious reach across international borders into free-media zones.

### Draconian Decrees and the Threat of Imprisonment

Simultaneously, the Musharraf administration backed its technological censorship with aggressive legal repression. Amendments were introduced to the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) ordinance, effectively criminalizing critical journalism. The new rules prohibited live broadcasts of political rallies, street protests, and violence, while explicitly banning any content deemed to "defame" the head of state, the military, or the executive branch.

Violating these draconian measures carried devastating penalties. Journalists, editors, and station owners faced heavy financial fines, the permanent revocation of their broadcasting licenses, the confiscation of equipment, and prison sentences of up to three years. 

Across Pakistan, police and intelligence agents raided news offices and confiscated transmission gear. Prominent journalists who refused to comply were harassed, detained, or placed under house arrest. A pervasive culture of fear took hold, designed to force self-censorship upon any reporter who dared to question the legitimacy of the emergency decree.

### Resistance and the Legacy of the Blackout

Despite the severe risks, Pakistani journalists launched a courageous resistance. Barred from the airwaves, GEO-TV and ARY reporters continued to gather news, taking to the streets with megaphones to read news bulletins to crowds of citizens. Newsrooms pivoted to primitive web-streaming services, blogs, and audio feeds over phone lines to bypass the satellite ban. Black-ribbon protests were organized outside press clubs across Islamabad, Karachi, and Lahore, resulting in mass arrests of media workers.

The international backlash was swift. Human rights organizations, press freedom watchdogs like the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and Reporters Without Borders (RSF), and foreign governments forcefully condemned the shutoff. Facing immense domestic unrest and diplomatic isolation, the government’s position rapidly deteriorated. ARY Digital was eventually allowed back on air after agreeing to modified broadcast guidelines, while GEO-TV held out longer, enduring massive financial losses before returning to the airwaves under intense scrutiny.

The 2007 media shutdown ultimately backfired on General Musharraf. Far from stabilizing his regime, the heavy-handed silencing of GEO-TV and ARY Digital alienated the middle class, united the political opposition, and shattered his reputation abroad. Within months, parliamentary elections were held, leading to the defeat of Musharraf's political allies and his eventual resignation from the presidency in August 2008.

The Gulf blackout stands as a watershed moment in the history of global media: a stark reminder of the lengths to which authoritarian governments will go to suppress truth, and a testament to the resilience of journalists determined to report it.

**Under Pakistani pressure, Dubai shuts down independent news networks GEO and ARY**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)** — Two of Pakistan’s largest independent television news networks have been forced completely off the air after authorities in the United Arab Emirates, yielding to intense pressure from President Gen. Pervez Musharraf’s regime, ordered them to cease broadcasting from Dubai. 

GEO TV and ARY Digital went dark late Friday night after officials at Dubai Media City—where the channels are headquartered—demanded they halt their transmissions. 

While Pakistani cable operators had already been ordered to block the channels domestically following Musharraf's November 3 declaration of emergency rule, this latest move cuts off the networks' satellite signals globally, leaving millions of overseas Pakistanis in the dark and striking a devastating blow to independent media in the region.

"We were given a deadline by the Dubai authorities, who made it clear they were acting under tremendous diplomatic pressure from the Pakistani government," said a senior GEO TV executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the situation. "This is an absolute tragedy for democracy and press freedom in Pakistan."

### Sweeping Crackdown on Dissent

General Musharraf, who seized power in a bloodless military coup in 1999, declared a state of emergency two weeks ago, citing rising Islamic militancy and an intrusive judiciary. Since the decree, his government has suspended the constitution, jailed thousands of political dissidents, lawyers, and human rights activists, and purged the nation's Supreme Court.

Central to the regime’s crackdown has been a severe new media ordinance. Under the new rules, media outlets face heavy fines, confiscation of equipment, and up to three years in prison if they broadcast content that brings the military or the presidency into "disrepute." 

Because both GEO TV and ARY Digital refused to sign a strict government-mandated code of conduct that effectively barred critical reporting of the emergency rule, Islamabad targeted their foreign transmission hubs.

Pakistani Information Minister Tariq Azim defended the government's stance, arguing that private media channels had crossed the line into inciting political instability.

"No sovereign nation can allow media networks to undermine state institutions or spread panic during a national crisis," Azim told reporters in Islamabad earlier this week. "Freedom of expression comes with responsibility."

### Protests and International Outcry

Journalists took to the streets in major Pakistani cities, including Islamabad, Karachi, and Lahore, on Saturday to protest the total news blackout. Protesters chanted anti-Musharraf slogans, demanding an immediate end to emergency rule and the restoration of independent news broadcasts.

GEO TV, in particular, had become a thorn in the military government's side over the past year. Its aggressive coverage of opposition rallies and popular talk shows—such as *Capital Talk*, hosted by prominent journalist Hamid Mir—helped fuel widespread public opposition to Musharraf’s rule.

The shutdown has also raised troubling questions about Dubai's reputation as a safe haven for international media outlets. Dubai Media City, launched in 2001, has aggressively marketed itself as a free-zone hub for global news organizations.

Media freedom advocacy groups quickly condemned the UAE’s decision to comply with Islamabad's demands.

"By capitulating to General Musharraf's authoritarian demands, the UAE authorities have severely damaged their credibility as a regional media hub," the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) said in a statement released Saturday. 

### Washington Expresses Concern

The shutdown comes at a delicate time for Washington, which views Musharraf as an indispensable ally in the fight against al Qaeda and the Taliban along the Afghan border. 

U.S. officials have increasingly voiced frustration with Musharraf’s authoritarian turn, calling for the immediate lifting of the emergency, the release of political detainees, and the restoration of a free press ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for January.

However, the Bush administration has so far resisted calls from Capitol Hill to condition or cut off billions of dollars in U.S. military aid to the nuclear-armed nation.

With GEO and ARY silenced, Pakistanis are left primarily with state-run PTV, which has offered glowing coverage of the government's actions. Opposition leaders, including former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, who was briefly placed under house arrest earlier this week, warned that a free election is impossible without a free media.

"A blackout of the press is a blackout of democracy," Bhutto told reporters outside her residence in Islamabad. "General Musharraf is trying to hide the truth from the Pakistani people, but you cannot rule a country by turning off the lights."

For years, channels like Geo News and ARY operated out of Dubai Media City to bypass stringent broadcasting regulations inside Pakistan. But late Friday, UAE telecommunication authorities, acting on requests from the Pakistani government, ordered the networks to cease transmissions immediately.

"By capitulating to the demands of General Musharraf, the UAE authorities have compromised Dubai's standing as an international media hub," said Joel Simon, executive director of CPJ. "This sets a dangerous precedent for press freedom throughout the Gulf region."

### Government defends crackdown

Pakistan's Ministry of Information defended the crackdown, accusing the private networks of violating broadcasting rules and airing content that threatened national security.

Speaking to reporters in Islamabad, a Pakistani government spokesman denied that the state was censoring legitimate news, claiming the networks had engaged in "sensationalism" that fueled political instability during a delicate period of transition.

Under new media regulations passed by Musharraf’s government under the emergency decree, broadcasters face up to three years in prison and heavy fines for airing material deemed critical of the military or the presidency. Most private domestic news networks remain off the air within Pakistan, leaving state-run PTV as the primary source of television news.

### Protests in Pakistan

Outside the blacked-out studios of Geo TV and ARY in Karachi and Islamabad, dozens of journalists gathered Saturday to protest the global shutdown, carrying placards reading "Stop Media Blockade" and chanting slogans against the emergency rule.

Executives at both networks said they were exploring legal remedies in Dubai to get back on the air, while attempting to ramp up news delivery via written web updates and audio streaming.

"They can pull our satellite feed," one Geo TV journalist told CNN via phone from Karachi, speaking on condition of anonymity. "But they cannot stop the truth from getting out."

**DUBAI, United Arab Emirates** — In a sharp rebuke of what he termed an unprecedented blow to international press freedom, Geo TV Network President Imran Aslan strongly condemned the decision by Dubai authorities to force Geo-TV and ARY Digital off the air, yielding to intense pressure from General Pervez Musharraf’s military regime in Pakistan.

The shutdown, executed late Friday night in Dubai Media City, silenced the uplink signals for the international broadcasts of both Geo News and ARY One World. The move effectively cut off millions of overseas South Asians from independent coverage of the expanding political crisis in Pakistan, following General Musharraf’s declaration of a state of emergency on November 3, 2007.

Speaking to journalists outside Geo TV’s Dubai operations center shortly after the transmission went black, a visibly dismayed Imran Aslan described the order as a black day for global media and an erosion of Dubai’s reputation as a safe haven for independent journalism.

"We are deeply shocked and saddened that Dubai Media City, a zone established on the very promise of freedom of expression, has succumbed to authoritarian arm-twisting from Islamabad," Aslan said. "This is not just an attack on Geo or ARY; it is an assault on the fundamental right of the public to know the truth during one of the most critical moments in Pakistan's history."

### Diplomatic Arm-Twisting in Dubai

According to network insiders, officials from the Dubai Technology and Media Free Zone Authority (TECOM) verbally informed the management of both networks that their news operations must immediately cease transmission. Sources within Geo revealed that the UAE authorities faced immense diplomatic pressure from General Musharraf, who allegedly threatened to disrupt UAE business interests in Pakistan—including major telecom and banking ventures—if the Dubai-based uplinks were not terminated.

Prior to the Dubai ban, the Musharraf administration had already pulled all private news channels off the domestic airwaves in Pakistan, leaving only the state-run Pakistan Television (PTV) to broadcast official regime updates. However, Geo and ARY had managed to bypass the domestic ban by continuing their live international broadcasts from Dubai, which were then picked up via satellite dishes and streamed online by millions of viewers worldwide.

Aslan confirmed that the Pakistani government had demanded Geo sign a new, highly restrictive 14-point "code of conduct" as a condition for resuming domestic operations. The code explicitly forbade criticizing General Musharraf, the military, or the judiciary. 

"We were given an ultimatum: surrender our journalistic integrity or face complete shutdown," Aslan declared. "Geo Network, under the vision of our leadership and the commitment of our staff, refused to sign away our editorial independence. Because we refused to compromise in Islamabad, the pressure was brought to bear right here in Dubai."

### A Double Blow to Independent Media

The shutdown simultaneously targeted ARY Digital’s news channel, ARY One World, which shared a similar fate after refusing to pull its live talk shows and reporting on civilian protests, lawyer movements, and the detention of Supreme Court judges in Pakistan.

Aslan expressed solidarity with ARY, highlighting that the dual shutdown demonstrated a coordinated campaign to completely obliterate independent Pakistani journalism.

"Today, two major voices of the Pakistani diaspora and the global community have been forcibly silenced," Aslan said. "For years, Dubai told the world that media networks could operate here without fear of political interference from foreign governments. Today’s actions shatter that pledge and set a dangerous precedent for international broadcasters based in the region."

### Newsrooms Under Siege

Despite the dark screens across satellite networks, Aslan emphasized that Geo’s newsroom staff in both Dubai and Pakistan would continue to report the news. Journalists at Geo’s Dubai bureau were seen continuing to edit packages and update web platforms, refusing to lay down their equipment.

"The screens may be black, but our pens are not dry and our voices are not silent," Aslan urged. "We are exploring every legal, technical, and operational avenue to restore our signal to our viewers. We owe it to the people of Pakistan who are risking their lives on the streets for democracy."

International media watchdogs, including the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) and Reporters Without Borders (RSF), immediately echoed Aslan’s outrage, calling on the UAE government to reverse its decision and allow the networks to resume broadcasting without delay.

As night fell over Dubai Media City, the usually bustling studios of Geo and ARY stood unusually quiet, marked only by the defiant words of its network president.

"Governments come and go, regimes fall, but the truth remains," Aslan concluded. "Geo was built on the trust of its audience, and no degree of censorship—whether engineered in Islamabad or executed in Dubai—will change our commitment to that trust."

**THE GLOBAL POST**

**Media Silenced in Pakistan: Musharraf Extends Emergency Crackdown to Dubai, Arrests Dozens of Journalists**

**By** Aamir Shah  
**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — November 17, 2007

In a dramatic escalation of his crackdown on free speech, Pakistan’s military ruler, General Pervez Musharraf, has extended his state of emergency beyond national borders, successfully pressuring authorities in the United Arab Emirates to shut down the Dubai-based operations of Pakistan’s top independent news networks.

The silencing of GEO TV and ARY Digital—the nation’s two most prominent private broadcasters—marks the deepest blow yet to Pakistan’s once-vibrant news media. The move comes amid widespread arrests of journalists, lawyers, and political activists across major Pakistani cities following Musharraf’s suspension of the constitution on November 3.

### Shadow over Dubai Media City

While domestic cable operators were forced to pull GEO and ARY off the air immediately after the emergency was declared, both networks had continued to broadcast to international audiences and online via satellite from their studios in Dubai Media City. 

However, late Friday night, UAE authorities ordered the networks to halt news broadcasts after intense diplomatic pressure from Islamabad. By Saturday morning, millions of viewers across the globe, including the vast Pakistani diaspora, were met with black screens.

"We have been told by the UAE government to stop our transmissions," said Hamid Mir, a senior executive and popular talk show host for GEO News, speaking via phone from Islamabad. "This is not just a crackdown inside Pakistan; General Musharraf is exporting his censorship abroad. They want an absolute blackout of truth."

Information Ministry officials in Islamabad defended the move, accusing the private networks of broadcasting "bias, sensationalism, and anti-state propaganda" that threatened national security. 

### Sweeping Restrictions and Mass Arrests

Since the declaration of the emergency, General Musharraf has imposed stringent new amendments to the Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) ordinance. The new laws grant the state sweeping powers to confiscate equipment, revoke licenses, and impose heavy prison terms for coverage deemed to "defame or ridicule" the president, the armed forces, or the executive. Live coverage of suicide bombings and political protests has been completely banned.

On the streets of Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad, the media response has been met with heavy-handed police brutality. Over the past week, riot police armed with batons have clashed with protesting media workers. 

In Karachi, police raided press clubs and arrested dozens of journalists demonstrating against the media blackout. Similar scenes played out in Islamabad, where officers bundled prominent commentators into police vans as they wore black armbands and chanted slogans demanding press freedom. Human rights groups estimate that over 100 journalists have been detained nationwide since the emergency began.

"General Musharraf is waging a war against his own civil society," said Ali Dayan Hasan, a South Asia researcher for Human Rights Watch. "By arresting journalists and shutting down independent channels, the regime is trying to crush any opposition to an illegal hold on power."

### A Regime in Crisis

General Musharraf has justified the emergency rule—and the accompanying media blackout—as a necessary measure to combat rising Islamic militancy and end what he termed "judicial interference" by the Supreme Court. However, political analysts widely view the crackdown as a desperate bid by Musharraf to secure his presidency before a high-court ruling could disqualify his recent re-election.

Before being placed under house arrest, deposed Chief Justice Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry called on the public to resist the military regime. With independent television silenced, state-run PTV remains the sole broadcast news source in the country, airing patriotic songs and government press releases.

The censorship has left a dangerous information vacuum. Millions of Pakistanis are turning to shortwave radio, international news websites, and text messaging to bypass state censorship, though rumor and anxiety are sweeping the nation.

International condemnation has been swift. Washington, a major backer of Musharraf in the "War on Terror," called the closure of the Dubai networks a "step backward" for Pakistani democracy, while the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) demanded the immediate release of all detained news workers.

Despite the pressure, network executives at GEO and ARY say they are fighting the shutdown order through legal channels in Dubai, but remain uncertain when—or if—they will be allowed to broadcast again. 

For now, the screens across Pakistan remain dark, symbolising the darkest era for press freedom in the country in a generation.
